newsitem.title: CHINA: China speculative funds said flowing to stamps.
newsitem.headline: China speculative funds said flowing to stamps.

text.p: China's crackdown on the stock markets and lower interest rates have sent hot money eager for a new target for speculation flooding into the stamp market, an official and dealers said on Wednesday.
"The risk for stocks (after the crackdown) is greater and common people don't really understand the stock market," said Chang Liancheng, manager of the Yuetan stamp market, Beijing's largest.
"Stamps are more tangible so more people buy them," he said in an interview.
China moved to cool stock speculation through tough measures at the beginning of May after the Shanghai and Shenzhen markets soared roughly 50 percent in the first four months of the year.

Economic reforms and rising income levels boosted China's stamp market in the past 10 years and trading fuelled by huge individual savings soared before Beijing gave its approval to stock markets in 1992.
The crackdown on the stock market coupled with two interest rate cuts in 1996 have triggered a new boom, Chang said.
"Since interest rates came down, buying stamps is more profitable than putting money in the bank," he said.
China cut interest rates twice last year, in May and August, to help struggling state enterprises.

Chang said the volume of business in Beijing's stamp market was difficult to determine because many unofficial dealers were taking part and some stamps could change hands up to eight times in a day, making it hard to monitor transactions.

However, one indication of the scale of the market was a decision to move this week from its open-air site in the Yuetan Park -- or Park of the Altar of the Moon -- in western Beijing to a bigger space.
Since Sunday, the market has been housed in a 12,284 square metre (40,300 square ft) warehouse rented from a furniture company in a northern suburb of the capital.

The number of registered dealers had jumped from around 700 in the Park of the Altar of the Moon to more than 1,300, while an unknown number of unregistered sellers also wandered the aisles of the market, Chang said.
Dealers and collectors said business had improved in recent weeks, but were hesitant to discuss the possibility that stamps had become China's new speculative vehicle.
Collectors spun tales of huge gains in trading of stamps.
"All that talk about money coming from the stock market is just a rumour," said one dealer. "But business is not bad."
Dealers appeared confident that their business was unlikely to become a target of an official crackdown.
"I'm not afraid of government intervention," said Chang. "The stamp market is still too small and it does not affect the national economy or people's livelihood."
